WORRY GUIDE — LIFE

When you're torn over whether to go

You type a reply to an invitation and delete it — it's been three days. You thought you had decided to go, but on the morning itself your body feels heavy. Decide not to go instead, and now you spend the whole day dragging around the thought that you should have gone after all. Going or not going should be a small choice, yet somehow it wears you down this much. To be clear at the outset, what you need to decide is not only whether to go. Deciding includes not continuing to think about the other side afterward. This page guides you through how to decide that way.

POINT 01

What's making this hard

When you're torn over whether to go, what is wavering is not always only your feelings about the plan itself. The reason you feel you don't want to go may actually be how much energy you have left, resistance to travel costs or fees, or tiredness from constantly fitting in with the other person. While the reasons stay mixed together, both options look heavy. Another factor is guilt about saying no. You don't want to disappoint the person who invited you, and you don't want to be thought unsociable. When that feeling is strong, you end up thinking not about whether you want to go, but about whether you are allowed to say no. And then there is the fear of being left out if you don't go — the imagination that something enjoyable might happen in a place where you are not. In most cases, what's making this hard is one of these three, or all of them.

POINT 02

How to sort it out

First, write your current feelings out in three parts: reasons you want to go, reasons you don't want to go, and whether you could go if the conditions changed. The third one matters, because a plan is not always a two-way choice. Arrive late, leave early, show your face only briefly. If it is simply that the current shape of the plan doesn't fit, changing the shape becomes the answer. This writing goes more easily if you do it while drawing a card and looking at it. The card you draw does not decide go or don't go; it is a mirror reflecting your current state. Are you tired, moving out of a sense of obligation, or actually looking forward to it? Once you can see your state, sorting the reasons out becomes faster. If you keep what you wrote in a log, it helps the next time you are torn over the same kind of invitation. Last time going was the right call; last time saying no let you rest. A record of your own decisions shortens the time you spend torn next time.

POINT 03

How to read the cards

When you're torn over whether to go, cards that speak to balance, moving forward, holding off, lightness, and time alone can offer useful clues.

The Two of Swords shows someone with eyes closed, balancing two swords. It reflects your current state itself — frozen, unable to lean either way.

The Chariot is a young figure holding the reins and moving forward by their own will. It helps you distinguish whether the source of your energy when you decide to go is obligation or motivation.

The Hanged Man shows someone hanging upside down on purpose to change their perspective. It points to the option of not deciding right away, holding off and seeing how things go.

The Fool is a young figure stepping out lightly with a single bundle. It asks not whether you have to go, but whether you feel you would like to try going.

The Hermit is a sage standing alone with a lantern. It points to the possibility that choosing not to go is not laziness, but time to restore yourself.

POINT 04

Questions to ask yourself

Try answering the following questions. If you had to name one reason you want to go, what would it be? Is the reason you don't want to go the plan itself, or your energy and money? If you could make the time shorter, would the desire to go come back? If you said no, what are you afraid of — the other person's reaction, or the imagined fear of being left out? When you have been torn the same way before, which choice did you make more often? After that choice, did the regret last long? Once your answers are together, all that is left is to decide. And once you have decided, don't keep thinking about the side you didn't choose. That is what deciding for yourself means.

FAQ

Frequently asked questions

When I'm torn over whether to go, what should I base the decision on?

Divide the reason you don't want to go into whether it is resistance to the content itself, or resistance to the hassle and social tiredness. The former can be material for saying no, but the latter is often a passing feeling that disappears on the morning itself. Which one is making you torn changes the answer.

What kinds of invitations do people tend to regret missing?

Gatherings with a group that will never assemble the same way again, or milestone occasions, tend to leave regret when you are absent. Regular gatherings, by contrast, tend to leave less regret because there will be a next time. Whether there is a next time is a practical yardstick when you are torn.

Is there a way to decline an invitation without giving offense?

The longer you explain your reasons, the more it sounds like an excuse. Say briefly that you already have plans that day, and if you can, offer an alternative occasion yourself — that makes the relationship easier to keep. More than declining itself, vagueness in how you decline is what damages a relationship.

Go, or not go? Why not sort out, through the questions the cards raise, your wish to value both the plans you were invited to and your time alone?
